clue.text: Consumer of dairy products gets extremely earnest after two ures

indicators.note: after sends the piece it governs to the end, behind the two blunders

parts.note: the scan has lost the start of a word, evidently 'failures': a miss and a muff are both failures

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of a word, so only its two end letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of earnest

explanation.surface: Someone who eats a lot of cheese and yoghurt turns serious after a couple of setbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue survives only as 'two ures' in the scan; read it as 'two failures', two words for a blunder placed before the ends of earnest.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme, little Miss Muffet sat on a tuffet eating her curds and whey, both milk products.

clue.text: Spells sorcerers with a c

parts.note: magi are wise men or sorcerers
the letter c, taken as written

explanation.surface: A spelling rule: the word for sorcerers is written with a c.
explanation.definitionFit: Spells cast by a wizard are acts of magic, so the plural noun and the mass noun share the sense of enchantment.

clue.text: Feel suspicious — let alarms off

indicators.note: when alarms go off things are thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Uneasy, someone sets off the burglar alarms.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to sense that something underhand is going on, which is to have a suspicion.

clue.text: Dubious dealings yield firm under a thousand in cash

indicators.note: in a down entry, being under something means coming after it in the grid

parts.note: a monkey is British slang for 500 pounds, a sum under a thousand
a firm is a business

explanation.surface: Shady deals produce a company worth less than a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: A monkey is London money slang for 500 pounds; the clue loosely calls it a sum under a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom refers to mischievous or underhand behaviour, the kind of shady trickery suggested by dubious dealings.

clue.text: Beetle found in meandering River Liffey

indicators.note: a meandering course twists and winds about, so the letters wander out of order

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
the Dublin river, taken as written

explanation.surface: An insect turns up in the winding River Liffey in Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: The glowing insect known by this name is in fact a beetle of the family Lampyridae, not a fly.

clue.text: Ruler sets up a representative in the capital

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting up means turning the letters upwards, so they read bottom to top
in places one item inside another, here the representative inside the city

parts.note: the capital city, here of Italy (and of the ancient empire)
rep is short for representative

explanation.surface: A ruler installs an agent in the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the whole word is written upwards, so the container is built first and then read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the sovereign ruler of an empire, such as the emperors who reigned from Rome.

clue.text: Strap about to administer a hard blow

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taws (or tawse) is a Scottish leather strap once used to punish schoolchildren

explanation.surface: A teacher's belt is about to deliver a hard stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: Taws is the Scottish schoolteacher's leather strap, a word the solver may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: To swat is to strike sharply, as one hits a fly, so it means delivering a hard smack.

clue.text: Cry about nothing — get hit

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the hit goes round the nothing

parts.note: to whop is to strike or thrash
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone weeps over nothing and gets slapped.
explanation.walkthrough: Whop is a less familiar spelling of whap or whack, meaning to hit hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A whoop is a loud shout of joy or excitement, a kind of cry.

clue.text: Nests seen as a possible source of anxiety

definitions.note: tenseness is the anxiety itself rather than its source; the clue is loose

indicators.note: possible hints at a potential version of the words, one rearrangement among many

parts.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Birds' nests are looked on as a cause of worry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenseness is a state of nervous strain, closely tied to anxiety and worry.

clue.text: Cockney's case of fruit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Cockney rhyming slang for stairs, as in a staircase
second meaning: two common orchard fruits

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of fruit' reads as a crate at a market stall, but 'case' is short for staircase; in Cockney rhyming slang, stairs are named by a rhyming phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang replaces stairs with a phrase that rhymes with it, and the phrase literally names two orchard fruits.

clue.text: Field worker making changes — 16

indicators.note: making changes means altering the order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the officer in 16 down's answer, the word supplied by that clue's wordplay

explanation.surface: A farmhand is making alterations.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the officer word inside the answer to 16 down, not the whole of that answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gleaner gathers leftover grain from a field after the harvest, so is literally a worker in the fields.

clue.text: Junk food is, with dad, a sore point

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
a corn is a painful patch of hard skin on the foot

explanation.surface: Fast food, along with Father, is a touchy subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sore point' suggests a touchy subject, but here it is a literal sore spot on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Popcorn is a cheap snack, the kind of salty nibble usually filed under junk eating.

clue.text: Picked up as necessary

definitions.meaning: first meaning: collected, as a parcel is fetched from a shop
second meaning: required or appropriate in the circumstances

explanation.definitionFit: Something collected has been fetched by its owner, and something required or warranted by the situation is likewise demanded.

clue.text: Surveillance, when one's withdrawn, in retrospect is a failure

indicators.note: in retrospect means looking back, so the remaining letters are read backwards
withdrawing one means removing a letter that stands for one

parts.note: espial is the act of spying or watching
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Looking back, spying with an agent pulled out was a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: Espial is an old word for spying; take out its I and turn ESPAL round.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or failure, such as a lapse of concentration or of memory.

clue.text: In other words, apply friction

parts.note: sc, short for Latin scilicet, means namely, introducing other words for the same thing
to rub is to apply friction

explanation.surface: Put another way, a physics lesson: create friction.
explanation.walkthrough: SC is the abbreviation for scilicet, used like 'that is' or 'namely'; read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer, a harder way of rubbing.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrub is to clean by rubbing hard, so it is rubbing put another way.

clue.text: Additional information one's turned up on transport

indicators.note: in a down entry, on means placed above what follows
in a down entry, turned up means the letters run upwards, read backwards

parts.note: I for one, plus the s of the apostrophe
transport in the sense of rapture or delight

explanation.surface: Someone's extra facts appeared on the bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' wants to mean a vehicle; it is the emotional sense, joy.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidelight is incidental information that throws extra light on a subject from an unexpected angle.

clue.text: County side bowls batsman out — he's without a single run

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the pronoun goes round the other letters

parts.note: to york a batsman is to bowl him out with a yorker, a ball pitched at his feet
taken as written
I as the numeral one
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A county cricket team's bowler dismisses a batsman who has failed to score even one.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a yorker is a ball aimed at the batsman's feet; the verb york means to dismiss with one. IR goes inside HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire is an English county with a famous first-class cricket team, so a county side in cricketing terms.

clue.text: Usually fashionable officer

parts.note: in means fashionable
a general is a senior army officer

explanation.surface: A stylish officer, as is normally the case.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means as a rule or for the most part, which is how things normally happen.

clue.text: It records the time a match's taken in the mist

indicators.note: being taken in means being enclosed, so one part sits inside the other

parts.note: the first letter of the outer word
a test is a test match, an international cricket game
the rest of the outer word

explanation.surface: A firework or match goes off in the fog, and something logs when it happened.
explanation.walkthrough: The mist is DAMP, a word for moist air; A TEST goes inside it after the D. A Test is a full international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: A date stamp prints the date on a document, so it records when something arrived or was dealt with.

clue.text: Loser's "Well run!" accepted by man

indicators.note: something accepted by another is taken inside it

parts.note: the first part of a man's name
well and so both open a sentence as fillers
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
the rest of the man's name

explanation.surface: A beaten runner is congratulated with a well-run race by a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The man is ALAN; SO and R go inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse that finishes out of the places, and by extension anyone who loses or fails.

clue.text: For every smoke there's a smell

parts.note: per means for each
fume is smoke or vapour

explanation.surface: Wherever there's smoke, an odour follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfume is a scent or fragrance, a pleasant smell.

clue.text: 5's drink
Left port with a cargo

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
Aden is a port in Yemen

explanation.surface: A ship departed harbour carrying freight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left port' reads as a ship sailing; Left is L, and port is the Yemeni harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Laden means loaded or weighed down, as a ship is when carrying its goods.

clue.text: Fancy woman, upset, put under doctor

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting one part under another means writing it after

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the name reads upwards

parts.note: Mae is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A man's mistress, distressed, is placed in a doctor's care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy woman' looks like one phrase for a mistress; Fancy alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To dream of something is to fancy or imagine it, and a dream is likewise a fancy.

clue.text: What comes from shaving — a small part in G & S

parts.note: a scrap is a small piece
taken as written
the two letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: An actor gets a bit part in a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta, after a shave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A small part in G & S' sounds like a minor role in a Gilbert and Sullivan opera, but every word is read literally in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaving wood or metal produces thin bits scraped off the surface, the scrapings.

clue.text: Parties with leaders of such integrity deserve electoral success

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Honest political parties ought to win at the ballot box.
explanation.definitionFit: Sides are the opposing groups in a contest or dispute, just as parties are.

clue.text: A bit of an ogre, a service mechanic

indicators.note: a bit of points to a stretch of letters lying within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across ogre, a and service

explanation.surface: A garage mechanic is a bit of a brute.
explanation.definitionFit: A greaser is slang for a motor mechanic, someone who greases engines.

clue.text: Not published in a rude form

indicators.note: a rude form is a crude new shape, so these letters take a different order

parts.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Something too vulgar to print stays unpublished.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaired means not broadcast or made public, as an unaired programme or opinion has not been released.

clue.text: Prison sentence — release put back

indicators.note: putting something back means sending it backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: to emit is to release or send out

explanation.surface: A jail term with the prisoner's release postponed.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time is slang for serving a term in jail, so the word means a prison term.

clue.text: Asks too little for foreign articles — seconds — after deception

indicators.note: after places the seconds behind the deception in the order

parts.note: un is French for a and der is German for the
a sell is a hoax or swindle
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A trader charges too little for imported goods, having been fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' sounds like goods for sale; here it is the grammar sense, words for a and the in other languages.
explanation.definitionFit: To undersell is to sell something for less than its value, asking too low a price.
